who-owns-an-effect.text: A contributor adding a mutable cell, a worker thread or an environment read wants to know where it belongs, who releases it and what check will ask about it. A reviewer wants to see each effect's owner, lifetime and reason in one place instead of reconstructing them from imports. This page is that map: what the census covers, which effects are allowed where, which way the module boundaries run, what evidence backs each predecessor ticket, and what stays openly unfulfilled.

the-story-this-serves.text: As a contributor, I add a counter to a command, a retry loop to a client or a coordination flag to a test, and the ownership check tells me exactly which file to classify it in, what to write beside it and what happens if I do not — before the review starts.

As a reviewer, I open this page and can tell which effects are necessary, who owns them, how long they live and which conformance-state work is still unfulfilled — without reading four hundred modules.

As an integrator, I learn that the product is single-threaded unless a written reason says otherwise, that no thread outlives its command, and that the unsafe escape hatch is absent from the tree — each with the check that would catch a regression.

what-the-census-covers.text: The census discovers every Haskell source by walking the tree — no per-file list — and puts each in exactly one structural category. Anything it cannot classify fails the run instead of slipping through.

455 sources in total. The census establishes structural facts — which files can name which effects — and never runtime behavior. That a module can name a mutable cell says nothing about what it does with it; what a command does is settled by the cage tests, the journeys and the hosted runs below, not here.

which-effects-are-gated-and-which-only-r.text: Which effects are gated, and which only recorded.

A gated effect needs a file-level entry in the ownership allowlist naming its owner, lifetime, access model and reason. A new file naming one without an entry fails; an entry whose effect is gone fails as stale.

Three rows deserve emphasis. No module imports the unsafe IO library, so no unsafe escape exists in the tree; the control that plants one proves the check rejects it. No module calls forkIO; the product's only concurrency is the Async library's scoped combinators. No module uses STM; the one match for the word is a theorem name, not a transaction, which is why the STM class is import-anchored rather than token-anchored.

Two further surfaces are recorded by the census but enforced elsewhere. Timeout bounds belong to the calling-thread confirmation design, whose deadline tests own them. Environment reads belong to the explicit-input rule, whose release-build exclusion the release controls own. Their carriers are named in the evidence map below.

where-the-production-effects-live.text: Every production effect below is allowlisted with the prose beside its implementation. The allowlist is the machine register; this table is the reader's summary.

The two trie adapters used to read as mutable state smuggled into pure computations. They are compatibility adapters with named callers and no locking: sharing one across threads without external serialization is a defect, and the haddock above each constructor says so.

why-the-product-stays-single-threaded.text: The product runs on the calling thread unless a written, compelling reason says otherwise, and no thread outlives the command that started it. Four sites carry such reasons, each beside its implementation with its join:
The devnet probe runs a node and a client together, joined before the probe returns.
The private facade serves sessions beside their followers, each session cancelling and joining its children before the next starts.
The conformance node runner holds one node-to-client thread per session, joined before the session ends.
The CLI-backend control bounds one confirmation wait with an explicit cancel, observed and joined before the run ends.

The test parallelism (two mapConcurrently_ shards over independent examples) and the test coordinations (entered/released/hold flags joined by withAsync before each example ends) are harness-owned: they run only under the suites, never in a release build. A newly introduced forkIO, async or concurrently site in a product package fails the ownership check until it is classified with its reason and its join.

which-way-dependencies-run.text: Effects flow one way: libraries expose capabilities, commands and runners compose them, tests drive them. Five boundaries hold this shape over the discovered extent — namespaces, not file lists, so a moved module is rechecked with nothing to edit:
the conformance library never imports the runner (the library stays runnable without live effects);
the offchain libraries never import the command layer (commands consume the libraries, never the reverse);
each journey executable keeps its local modules (old runners are never extended by sharing);
no ordinary executable links a host module (the adversary stays outside the release, its test-only reader excepted);
the command layer is imported only at composition — commands, applications and tests.

what-backs-the-predecessors-and-what-sta.text: What backs the predecessors, and what stays open.
Each row names the accepted evidence or the explicitly open requirement. Local paths are never public evidence; the hosted records below are.

how-to-change-effect-code.text: Write the owner, lifetime and reason beside the implementation, not only in the allowlist.
Regenerate the site binding from the tree and review its diff beside the code change; commit both together.
Run the ownership check and its controls; hosted CI repeats them at the candidate head.
A change touching the session, receipt or reconcile modules beyond comments needs the stacked follow-on lane's attention first; ask before growing there.
